questions.q: What is the difference between manual and automated classification tagging?
options: Manual tagging is always more accurate, so automated tagging should never be used
Manual tagging relies on a person's judgment to apply a label; automated tagging uses discovery techniques like pattern or metadata scanning to apply or recommend one without a required human step
Automated tagging only works on image files
There is no real difference; the terms are interchangeable
questions.explain: Manual tagging depends on a steward's judgment and is indispensable for ambiguous cases automation misses; automated tagging scales across an entire data estate but inherits the limits of the discovery technique behind it.

questions.q: Why does a classification label need to be stored as metadata rather than just known by a data steward?
options: Because metadata is required by law in every jurisdiction
Because a label only does real work if it's queryable and enforceable by other systems, not just documented knowledge in someone's head
Because metadata storage is cheaper than any other storage method
Because data stewards are not allowed to remember classification decisions
questions.explain: A label that exists only as a fact a person knows can't be read or acted on by the systems that need to enforce access restrictions, encryption, or logging — it has to be stored as queryable metadata.

questions.q: Per this lesson's inheritance rule, what classification should result when an Internal table is joined with a Confidential table?
options: Public, since combining data always reduces sensitivity
Internal, since that was the classification of the first table in the join
Confidential, since the combined dataset inherits the higher of the two classifications
The join is not allowed under any classification scheme
questions.explain: A dataset formed by joining or merging sources takes on the highest classification among them — the combined result is at least as sensitive as its most sensitive input.

questions.q: Which scenario illustrates the 'classification propagation' problem this lesson describes?
options: A Confidential table is exported to a spreadsheet for analysis, and the spreadsheet ends up unlabeled because the classification didn't travel with the copy
A Public dataset is accidentally deleted by an administrator
A classification scheme is renamed from four tiers to five tiers
A data steward manually reviews a dataset and confirms its existing label is correct
questions.explain: Propagation failures happen when data is copied, joined, or fed into a pipeline and the classification doesn't automatically carry forward — exactly the exported-spreadsheet scenario described.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a classification label that triggers no actual control 'isn't doing its job'?
options: Because a purely descriptive label that nothing acts on functions as a filing system, not a security control — the point of labeling is for it to trigger real, concrete controls like access restriction or encryption
Because labels must always be removed after 30 days
Because only Restricted-tier data is allowed to have a visible label
Because classification labels are purely a legal formality with no technical purpose
questions.explain: If a Restricted tag is visible in a catalog but nothing downstream reads it and acts on it, the organization has documentation, not protection — the label has to actually trigger access restrictions, encryption, or logging to matter.
